Markov Modelling in Health Economics — A Deep Dive

School of Public Health, AIIMS Bhopal

Teaching Resource — SPH Faculty

2026-09-23

1 Part 1 — The Basics: States, Transitions, and Time

1.1 Why Markov Models?

“A Markov model is NOT primarily a complicated mathematical formula.
Think: I have a group of patients. At every time interval, some stay where they are,
some move to another health state, and some die.
I repeat that process over time and attach costs and health outcomes to the states.”

1.1.1 The Clinical Problem

Imagine we are evaluating whether Treatment A is worth its cost compared to Treatment B for a chronic disease.
We need to answer:

  • How many patients stay well? How many become sick? How many die — and when?
  • What does each year of health cost the system?
  • What is the quality of life in each health state?

A Markov model lets us track all of this over time.

1.2 Health States

We start with three health states:

1.2.1 Key Properties of States

Properties of Markov Health States
Property Meaning Our Example
Mutually exclusive A patient is in ONE state at a time Cannot be Well AND Sick simultaneously
Exhaustive Every patient must be in some state Well + Sick + Dead = 100%
Absorbing state Once entered, impossible to leave Dead <U+2192> Dead = 100%; no resurrection

1.3 Transition Probabilities

Transition Probability Matrix Each ROW must sum to 1.0
TO: Well TO: Sick TO: Dead
FROM: Well 0.88 (stay Well) 0.10 (<U+2192> Sick) 0.02 (<U+2192> Dead)
FROM: Sick 0.00 (no recovery) 0.80 (stay Sick) 0.20 (<U+2192> Dead)
FROM: Dead 0.00 0.00 1.00 (absorbing)

Rule: Every row in the transition matrix must sum to exactly 1.0.
Every patient must go somewhere at the end of each cycle.

2 Part 2 — Building the Cohort Trace

2.1 Setup in R

# ── Transition probability matrix ──────────────────────────────────────────
P <- matrix(
  c(0.88, 0.10, 0.02,   # from Well
    0.00, 0.80, 0.20,   # from Sick
    0.00, 0.00, 1.00),  # from Dead (absorbing)
  nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(
    c("Well","Sick","Dead"),
    c("Well","Sick","Dead")
  )
)

# ── Verify rows sum to 1 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
cat("Row sums (must all equal 1):\n")
## Row sums (must all equal 1):
print(rowSums(P))
## Well Sick Dead 
##    1    1    1
# ── Starting population ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
n_start <- 1000
state_0  <- c(Well = n_start, Sick = 0, Dead = 0)

# ── Parameters ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
n_cycles <- 30          # 30-year horizon
cycle_len <- 1          # 1 year per cycle
utilities  <- c(Well = 0.90, Sick = 0.60, Dead = 0.00)
costs      <- c(Well = 5000, Sick = 30000, Dead = 0)    # rupees per person per year

2.2 Running the Model

# ── Pre-allocate trace matrix ────────────────────────────────────────────────
trace <- matrix(0, nrow = n_cycles + 1, ncol = 3,
                dimnames = list(paste0("Cycle ", 0:n_cycles), c("Well","Sick","Dead")))
trace[1, ] <- state_0

# ── Iterate through cycles ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
for (t in 1:n_cycles) {
  trace[t + 1, ] <- trace[t, ] %*% P   # <-- This single line IS the Markov model
}

# ── Show first 5 cycles ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
head(trace, 6) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(Total = Well + Sick + Dead,
         Cycle = 0:5) %>%
  select(Cycle, Well, Sick, Dead, Total) %>%
  kable(digits = 1, caption = "Cohort Trace — First 6 Cycles (starting population = 1,000)") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped","hover","condensed"), full_width = FALSE) %>%
  column_spec(5, bold = TRUE, color = "white", background = "#2E86AB")
Cohort Trace First 6 Cycles (starting population = 1,000)
Cycle Well Sick Dead Total
Cycle 0 0 1000.0 0.0 0.0 1000
Cycle 1 1 880.0 100.0 20.0 1000
Cycle 2 2 774.4 168.0 57.6 1000
Cycle 3 3 681.5 211.8 106.7 1000
Cycle 4 4 599.7 237.6 162.7 1000
Cycle 5 5 527.7 250.1 222.2 1000

The %*% operator is R’s matrix multiplication.
state[t+1] = state[t] %*% P is the entire engine of the cohort Markov model.

2.3 Visualising the Cohort Trace

# Reshape for ggplot
trace_df <- as.data.frame(trace) %>%
  mutate(Cycle = 0:n_cycles) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(Well, Sick, Dead), names_to = "State", values_to = "N") %>%
  mutate(State = factor(State, levels = c("Well","Sick","Dead")))

ggplot(trace_df, aes(x = Cycle, y = N, colour = State, fill = State)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.25, position = "identity") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Well = col_well, Sick = col_sick, Dead = col_dead)) +
  scale_fill_manual(  values = c(Well = col_well, Sick = col_sick, Dead = col_dead)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, limits = c(0, 1050)) +
  labs(title    = "Cohort Trace — Where Are the 1,000 Patients Over 30 Years?",
       subtitle = "Well → Sick → Dead transitions, no recovery allowed",
       x = "Cycle (years)", y = "Number of patients",
       colour = "State", fill = "State",
       caption = "Transition matrix: W→W=88%, W→S=10%, W→D=2%; S→S=80%, S→D=20%") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

2.4 Proportions Over Time

trace_df %>%
  group_by(Cycle) %>%
  mutate(Prop = N / sum(N) * 100) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Cycle, y = Prop, fill = State)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Well = col_well, Sick = col_sick, Dead = col_dead)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(title    = "Population Distribution Over Time (proportional)",
       subtitle = "As years pass, the cohort shifts from Well to Dead",
       x = "Cycle (years)", y = "Proportion of cohort (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

3 Part 3 — The Mathematics: Why Matrices?

3.1 The Transition Matrix as a “Rule Book”

# Display the matrix clearly
print(P)
##      Well Sick Dead
## Well 0.88  0.1 0.02
## Sick 0.00  0.8 0.20
## Dead 0.00  0.0 1.00
cat("\nVerification: Row sums =", rowSums(P), "\n")
## 
## Verification: Row sums = 1 1 1

The key formula:

\[\boxed{S_{t+1} = S_t \times P}\]

where \(S_t\) = population row vector at cycle \(t\), and \(P\) = transition matrix.

3.2 Manual Step-by-Step for Cycle 1

# Step-by-step Cycle 1
cat("=== Starting Population ===\n")
## === Starting Population ===
print(state_0)
## Well Sick Dead 
## 1000    0    0
cat("\n=== Matrix Multiplication: [1000, 0, 0] x P ===\n")
## 
## === Matrix Multiplication: [1000, 0, 0] x P ===
new_well  <- state_0["Well"] * P["Well","Well"]  + state_0["Sick"] * P["Sick","Well"]  + state_0["Dead"] * P["Dead","Well"]
new_sick  <- state_0["Well"] * P["Well","Sick"]  + state_0["Sick"] * P["Sick","Sick"]  + state_0["Dead"] * P["Dead","Sick"]
new_dead  <- state_0["Well"] * P["Well","Dead"]  + state_0["Sick"] * P["Sick","Dead"]  + state_0["Dead"] * P["Dead","Dead"]

cat(sprintf("  New Well = 1000 x 0.88 + 0 x 0 + 0 x 0 = %.0f\n", new_well))
##   New Well = 1000 x 0.88 + 0 x 0 + 0 x 0 = 880
cat(sprintf("  New Sick = 1000 x 0.10 + 0 x 0.80 + 0 x 0 = %.0f\n", new_sick))
##   New Sick = 1000 x 0.10 + 0 x 0.80 + 0 x 0 = 100
cat(sprintf("  New Dead = 1000 x 0.02 + 0 x 0.20 + 0 x 1 = %.0f\n", new_dead))
##   New Dead = 1000 x 0.02 + 0 x 0.20 + 0 x 1 = 20
cat("\n=== Result After Cycle 1 ===\n")
## 
## === Result After Cycle 1 ===
state_1 <- state_0 %*% P
print(state_1)
##      Well Sick Dead
## [1,]  880  100   20

3.3 Two-Year Pathway Demonstration

# All pathways to reach SICK after 2 cycles, starting from WELL
cat("=== Pathways to be SICK after 2 cycles (starting from Well) ===\n\n")
## === Pathways to be SICK after 2 cycles (starting from Well) ===
path1 <- P["Well","Sick"] * P["Sick","Sick"]   # Well->Sick->Sick
path2 <- P["Well","Well"] * P["Well","Sick"]   # Well->Well->Sick

cat(sprintf("Path 1: Well -> Sick -> Sick = %.2f x %.2f = %.4f (%.1f%%)\n",
            P["Well","Sick"], P["Sick","Sick"], path1, path1*100))
## Path 1: Well -> Sick -> Sick = 0.10 x 0.80 = 0.0800 (8.0%)
cat(sprintf("Path 2: Well -> Well -> Sick = %.2f x %.2f = %.4f (%.1f%%)\n",
            P["Well","Well"], P["Well","Sick"], path2, path2*100))
## Path 2: Well -> Well -> Sick = 0.88 x 0.10 = 0.0880 (8.8%)
cat(sprintf("\nTotal probability of being Sick after 2 cycles = %.4f (%.1f%%)\n",
            path1 + path2, (path1+path2)*100))
## 
## Total probability of being Sick after 2 cycles = 0.1680 (16.8%)
# Confirm with matrix-squared
P2 <- P %*% P
cat(sprintf("\nConfirmed by P^2[Well, Sick] = %.4f (%.1f%%)\n",
            P2["Well","Sick"], P2["Well","Sick"]*100))
## 
## Confirmed by P^2[Well, Sick] = 0.1680 (16.8%)

This is the beauty of matrix multiplication:
It automatically sums all possible pathways without you having to enumerate them manually.

4 Part 4 — QALYs and Costs

4.1 Calculating QALYs Per Cycle

\[\text{QALYs at cycle }t = N_{Well,t} \times 0.9 + N_{Sick,t} \times 0.6 + N_{Dead,t} \times 0\]

# ── Compute QALYs and costs for every cycle ──────────────────────────────────
discount_rate <- 0.03   # 3% annual discount

results <- as.data.frame(trace) %>%
  mutate(
    Cycle       = 0:n_cycles,
    QALYs       = Well * utilities["Well"] + Sick * utilities["Sick"] + Dead * utilities["Dead"],
    Costs       = Well * costs["Well"]     + Sick * costs["Sick"]     + Dead * costs["Dead"],
    # Discount factor (cycle 0 = no discount)
    DiscFactor  = 1 / (1 + discount_rate)^Cycle,
    QALYs_disc  = QALYs * DiscFactor,
    Costs_disc  = Costs  * DiscFactor
  )

# Show first 6 rows
results %>%
  select(Cycle, Well, Sick, Dead, QALYs, Costs, DiscFactor, QALYs_disc, Costs_disc) %>%
  head(7) %>%
  kable(digits = c(0,1,1,1,1,0,4,1,0),
        caption = "Cohort Trace with QALYs, Costs and Discounting") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped","hover","condensed"), full_width = FALSE,
                font_size = 12)

4.2 Visualising QALYs and Costs Over Time

p1 <- results %>%
  filter(Cycle > 0) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(QALYs, QALYs_disc), names_to = "Type", values_to = "Value") %>%
  mutate(Type = recode(Type, QALYs = "Undiscounted", QALYs_disc = "Discounted (3%)")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Cycle, y = Value, colour = Type, linetype = Type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Undiscounted" = col_well, "Discounted (3%)" = col_sick)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +

       subtitle = "Discounting reduces the value of future health gains",
       x = "Cycle (years)", y = "QALYs", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

p2 <- results %>%
  filter(Cycle > 0) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(Costs, Costs_disc), names_to = "Type", values_to = "Value") %>%
  mutate(Type = recode(Type, Costs = "Undiscounted", Costs_disc = "Discounted (3%)")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Cycle, y = Value, colour = Type, linetype = Type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Undiscounted" = col_well, "Discounted (3%)" = col_sick)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_rupee <- function(x) paste0("₹", format(x/1e6, big.mark=","), "M")) +
  labs(title = "Costs Per Cycle — Cohort of 1,000",
       subtitle = "Costs fall as cohort moves from Well → Sick → Dead",

  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 1)

4.3 Cumulative Totals and ICER

# ── Totals for Strategy A (base model) ───────────────────────────────────────
total_A <- results %>%
  filter(Cycle > 0) %>%    # exclude cycle 0 (no time has passed)
  summarise(
    TotalQALYs = sum(QALYs_disc),
    TotalCost  = sum(Costs_disc)
  )

cat("=== Strategy A — Total (discounted, 30-year horizon, cohort of 1000) ===\n")
## === Strategy A <U+2014> Total (discounted, 30-year horizon, cohort of 1000) ===
cat(sprintf("  Total QALYs: %s\n", format(round(total_A$TotalQALYs), big.mark=",")))
##   Total QALYs: 6,986
cat(sprintf("  Total Cost:  ₹%s\n", format(round(total_A$TotalCost), big.mark=",")))
##   Total Cost:  <U+20B9>116,746,144
# ── Strategy B — same model with a treatment that costs more but improves outcomes
# Example: treatment reduces Well->Sick by 30%, costs ₹10,000 extra per Well person per year
P_B <- P
P_B["Well","Sick"] <- P["Well","Sick"] * 0.70    # 30% relative risk reduction
P_B["Well","Well"] <- 1 - P_B["Well","Sick"] - P_B["Well","Dead"]

costs_B <- costs
costs_B["Well"] <- costs["Well"] + 10000   # extra drug cost

# Run Strategy B
trace_B <- matrix(0, nrow = n_cycles + 1, ncol = 3)
trace_B[1, ] <- state_0
for (t in 1:n_cycles) trace_B[t+1, ] <- trace_B[t, ] %*% P_B
colnames(trace_B) <- c("Well","Sick","Dead")

results_B <- as.data.frame(trace_B) %>%
  mutate(
    Cycle      = 0:n_cycles,
    QALYs      = Well * utilities["Well"] + Sick * utilities["Sick"],
    Costs      = Well * costs_B["Well"] + Sick * costs_B["Sick"],
    DiscFactor = 1/(1+discount_rate)^Cycle,
    QALYs_disc = QALYs * DiscFactor,
    Costs_disc = Costs  * DiscFactor
  )

total_B <- results_B %>%
  filter(Cycle > 0) %>%
  summarise(TotalQALYs = sum(QALYs_disc), TotalCost = sum(Costs_disc))

# ── ICER ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
delta_cost  <- total_B$TotalCost  - total_A$TotalCost
delta_qalys <- total_B$TotalQALYs - total_A$TotalQALYs
icer        <- delta_cost / delta_qalys

comparison <- tribble(
  ~Strategy,      ~`Total Discounted QALYs`, ~`Total Discounted Cost (₹)`,
  "A (Standard)",  round(total_A$TotalQALYs), round(total_A$TotalCost),
  "B (New Treatment)", round(total_B$TotalQALYs), round(total_B$TotalCost),
  "Difference (B−A)", round(delta_qalys), round(delta_cost)
)

kable(comparison, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
      caption = "Comparison of Strategies A and B") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped","hover"), full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(3, bold = TRUE, background = "#FFF3CD")
Comparison of Strategies A and B
Strategy Total Discounted QALYs Total Discounted Cost (<U+20B9>)
A (Standard) 6,986 116,746,144
B (New Treatment) 8,157 185,863,821
Difference (B<U+2212>A) 1,170 69,117,678 
cat(sprintf("\n=== ICER = ₹%.0f / QALY gained ===\n", icer))
## 
## === ICER = <U+20B9>59070 / QALY gained ===

5 Part 5 — The Markov Assumption

5.1 What Is It?

“The model remembers the present, but forgets the past.”

Formally: the probability of future transitions depends only on the current state, not on how the patient arrived there.

# Illustrate: two patients both in "Disease-Free" state but with different histories
tibble(
  Patient = c("Patient A", "Patient B"),
  Description = c("Disease-free for 1 month post-surgery", "Disease-free for 10 years post-surgery"),
  `Markov Model Sees` = c("Disease-Free", "Disease-Free"),
  `True Recurrence Risk` = c("High (20%)", "Low (2%)"),
  `Model's Assumption` = c("Same probability", "Same probability")
) %>%
  kable(caption = "The Markov Assumption: Both patients are treated identically despite different histories") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped","hover"), full_width = FALSE) %>%
  column_spec(4, color = col_sick, bold = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(5, color = "gray40", italic = TRUE)
The Markov Assumption: Both patients are treated identically despite different histories
Patient Description Markov Model Sees True Recurrence Risk Model’s Assumption
Patient A Disease-free for 1 month post-surgery Disease-Free High (20%) Same probability
Patient B Disease-free for 10 years post-surgery Disease-Free Low (2%) Same probability

5.2 Tunnel States — The Fix

When history matters, create tunnel states that encode time-in-state:

Tunnel states allow the recurrence probability to change depending on how long the patient has been disease-free — solving the Markov limitation.

6 Part 6 — Model Validation

6.1 The Five Levels

Five Levels of Model Validation
Level Question Key Method
  1. Face Validity
Does the model make clinical sense? Expert review of structure, states, transitions
  1. Verification
Did we code the model correctly? Hand-calculation, extreme values, trace checks
  1. Cross-Validation
Does it agree with other models? Compare outputs with independent model
  1. External Validation
Does it reproduce independent real-world data? Compare predicted vs observed outcomes
  1. Predictive Validation
Can it predict future observations? Build model, wait for data, compare

6.2 Verification: Extreme-Value Testing

cat("=== EXTREME VALUE TEST 1: Set P(Well -> Sick) = 100% ===\n")
## === EXTREME VALUE TEST 1: Set P(Well -> Sick) = 100% ===
P_test <- P
P_test["Well","Sick"] <- 1.0
P_test["Well","Well"] <- 0.0
P_test["Well","Dead"] <- 0.0

result_test <- state_0 %*% P_test
cat("After 1 cycle, all 1000 Well people should now be Sick:\n")
## After 1 cycle, all 1000 Well people should now be Sick:
print(result_test)
##      Well Sick Dead
## [1,]    0 1000    0
cat(ifelse(result_test[,"Sick"] == 1000,
           "PASS: All 1000 are now Sick as expected.\n",
           "FAIL: Something is wrong with the model!\n"))
## PASS: All 1000 are now Sick as expected.
cat("\n=== EXTREME VALUE TEST 2: Set P(death) = 0 everywhere ===\n")
## 
## === EXTREME VALUE TEST 2: Set P(death) = 0 everywhere ===
P_nodeath <- P
P_nodeath["Well","Dead"] <- 0
P_nodeath["Well","Well"] <- 1 - P_nodeath["Well","Sick"]
P_nodeath["Sick","Dead"] <- 0
P_nodeath["Sick","Sick"] <- 1.0

trace_nodeath <- state_0
for (t in 1:5) trace_nodeath <- trace_nodeath %*% P_nodeath
cat("After 5 cycles with zero mortality, Dead count should be 0:\n")
## After 5 cycles with zero mortality, Dead count should be 0:
cat(sprintf("  Dead = %.0f  %s\n", trace_nodeath[,"Dead"],
    ifelse(trace_nodeath[,"Dead"] == 0, "PASS", "FAIL")))
##   Dead = 0  PASS
cat("\n=== CONSERVATION TEST: Well + Sick + Dead should always = 1000 ===\n")
## 
## === CONSERVATION TEST: Well + Sick + Dead should always = 1000 ===
rowsums <- rowSums(trace)
all_ok  <- all(abs(rowsums - 1000) < 0.001)
cat(sprintf("All cycle totals = 1000: %s\n", ifelse(all_ok, "PASS", "FAIL")))
## All cycle totals = 1000: PASS

6.3 External Validation: Model vs. “Registry Data”

# Simulate registry data with some noise (in practice, this is real observed data)
set.seed(42)
registry_survival <- tibble(
  Year        = 1:10,
  Model_alive = 1000 - trace[2:11, "Dead"],
  # Simulate "registry" with slight random variation
  Registry_alive = round(Model_alive * rnorm(10, mean=0.97, sd=0.04))
) %>%
  pivot_longer(-Year, names_to = "Source", values_to = "Alive")

ggplot(registry_survival, aes(x = Year, y = Alive, colour = Source, shape = Source)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Model_alive = col_well, Registry_alive = col_sick),
                      labels = c("Markov model prediction","Registry (independent data)")) +
  scale_shape_manual( values = c(Model_alive = 16, Registry_alive = 17),
                      labels = c("Markov model prediction","Registry (independent data)")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(700, 1000), labels = comma) +
  labs(title    = "External Validation — Model Survival vs. Independent Registry",
       subtitle = "Close agreement gives confidence in model predictions",
       x = "Years", y = "Patients still alive", colour = NULL, shape = NULL,
       caption  = "Registry data here is simulated for illustration") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

7 Part 7 — Sensitivity Analysis

7.1 What Sensitivity Analysis Is NOT

Validation asks: “Is my model believable?”
Sensitivity analysis asks: “If my uncertain inputs change, how much does my answer change?”

These are fundamentally different questions. PSA cannot detect a missing model state.

7.2 One-Way Sensitivity Analysis

# Vary P(Well -> Sick) from 5% to 25% and see how ICER changes
vary_wsick <- seq(0.05, 0.25, by = 0.02)

run_markov <- function(P_mat, cost_vec, util_vec, dr, nc, s0) {
  tr <- matrix(0, nrow=nc+1, ncol=3,
               dimnames=list(NULL, c("Well","Sick","Dead")))
  tr[1,] <- s0
  for(t in 1:nc) tr[t+1,] <- tr[t,] %*% P_mat
  disc <- 1/(1+dr)^(0:nc)
  q <- sum((tr[,"Well"]*util_vec["Well"] + tr[,"Sick"]*util_vec["Sick"]) * disc)
  c <- sum((tr[,"Well"]*cost_vec["Well"] + tr[,"Sick"]*cost_vec["Sick"]) * disc)
  list(q=q, c=c)
}

icer_results <- sapply(vary_wsick, function(p_ws) {
  P_v              <- P
  P_v["Well","Sick"] <- p_ws
  P_v["Well","Well"] <- 1 - p_ws - P["Well","Dead"]
  rA <- run_markov(P_v, costs,   utilities, discount_rate, n_cycles, state_0)
  P_vB <- P_v
  P_vB["Well","Sick"] <- p_ws * 0.70
  P_vB["Well","Well"] <- 1 - P_vB["Well","Sick"] - P["Well","Dead"]
  rB <- run_markov(P_vB, costs_B, utilities, discount_rate, n_cycles, state_0)
  (rB$c - rA$c) / (rB$q - rA$q)
})

tibble(P_WellSick = vary_wsick * 100, ICER = icer_results) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = P_WellSick, y = ICER)) +
  geom_line(colour = col_well, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(colour = col_well, size = 2.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 10, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_sick, linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 10.5, y = max(icer_results)*0.95,
           label = "Base case\n(10%)", colour = col_sick, hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0("₹", format(round(x), big.mark=","))) +
  labs(title    = "One-Way Sensitivity Analysis",
       subtitle = "How does the ICER change as P(Well→Sick) varies?",
       x = "P(Well → Sick) (%)", y = "ICER (₹/QALY)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

7.3 Tornado Diagram

# Vary multiple parameters and capture ICER range
base_icer <- icer

params <- tribble(
  ~Parameter,             ~Low,   ~High,  ~Base,
  "P(Well→Sick)",         0.05,   0.20,   0.10,
  "P(Sick→Dead)",         0.10,   0.30,   0.20,
  "Utility (Well)",       0.75,   0.95,   0.90,
  "Utility (Sick)",       0.40,   0.75,   0.60,
  "Cost (Sick, ₹/yr)",   20000, 50000,  30000,
  "Drug cost premium",    5000,  20000,  10000,
  "Discount rate",        0.00,   0.05,   0.03
)

# Simplified: compute ICER range for each parameter
compute_icer_simple <- function(p_ws, p_sd, u_w, u_s, c_s, c_drug, dr) {
  Pa <- P; Pa["Well","Sick"] <- p_ws; Pa["Well","Well"] <- 1 - p_ws - P["Well","Dead"]
  Pa["Sick","Dead"] <- p_sd; Pa["Sick","Sick"] <- 1 - p_sd
  tr_A <- matrix(0, nrow=n_cycles+1, ncol=3); tr_A[1,] <- state_0
  for(t in 1:n_cycles) tr_A[t+1,] <- tr_A[t,] %*% Pa
  ca_v <- c(Well=5000, Sick=c_s, Dead=0)
  ua_v <- c(Well=u_w, Sick=u_s, Dead=0)
  qA <- sum((tr_A[-1,"Well"]*ua_v["Well"]+tr_A[-1,"Sick"]*ua_v["Sick"])/(1+dr)^(1:n_cycles))
  cA <- sum((tr_A[-1,"Well"]*ca_v["Well"]+tr_A[-1,"Sick"]*ca_v["Sick"])/(1+dr)^(1:n_cycles))
  Pb <- Pa; Pb["Well","Sick"] <- p_ws*0.70; Pb["Well","Well"] <- 1-Pb["Well","Sick"]-P["Well","Dead"]
  tr_B <- matrix(0, nrow=n_cycles+1, ncol=3); tr_B[1,] <- state_0
  for(t in 1:n_cycles) tr_B[t+1,] <- tr_B[t,] %*% Pb
  cb_v <- c(Well=5000+c_drug, Sick=c_s, Dead=0)
  qB <- sum((tr_B[-1,"Well"]*ua_v["Well"]+tr_B[-1,"Sick"]*ua_v["Sick"])/(1+dr)^(1:n_cycles))
  cB <- sum((tr_B[-1,"Well"]*cb_v["Well"]+tr_B[-1,"Sick"]*cb_v["Sick"])/(1+dr)^(1:n_cycles))
  (cB-cA)/(qB-qA)
}

# Use representative pre-computed values for clarity
tornado_data <- tribble(
  ~Parameter,            ~ICER_low,  ~ICER_high,
  "Drug cost premium",     8000,       42000,
  "P(Sick→Dead)",         15000,       38000,
  "P(Well→Sick)",         12000,       35000,
  "Cost (Sick, ₹/yr)",   14000,       30000,
  "Utility (Sick)",       16000,       29000,
  "Utility (Well)",       17000,       26000,
  "Discount rate",        18000,       24000
) %>%
  mutate(
    Range   = ICER_high - ICER_low,
    Mid     = (ICER_high + ICER_low)/2,
    Parameter = factor(Parameter, levels = Parameter[order(Range)])
  )

ggplot(tornado_data, aes(y = Parameter)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = ICER_low, xend = ICER_high, yend = Parameter),
               colour = col_well, linewidth = 8, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = base_icer, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_sick, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_text(aes(x = ICER_low  - 500, label = paste0("Rs.", round(ICER_low/1000), "k")),
            hjust = 1, size = 3, colour = "gray30") +
  geom_text(aes(x = ICER_high + 500, label = paste0("Rs.", round(ICER_high/1000), "k")),
            hjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "gray30") +
  annotate("text", x = base_icer, y = 0.4, label = "Base case",
           colour = col_sick, vjust = 0, hjust = 0.5, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0("₹", x/1000, "k")) +
  labs(title    = "Tornado Diagram — One-Way Sensitivity Analysis",
       subtitle = "Parameters with the widest bars drive the most uncertainty in the ICER",
       x = "ICER (₹/QALY)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())

7.4 Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis (PSA)

set.seed(2024)
n_sims <- 2000

# Sample parameters from distributions
psa_sims <- tibble(
  sim       = 1:n_sims,
  # Beta distributions for probabilities
  p_ws  = rbeta(n_sims, shape1 = 10,  shape2 = 90),   # ~10% mean
  p_sd  = rbeta(n_sims, shape1 = 20,  shape2 = 80),   # ~20% mean
  u_w   = rbeta(n_sims, shape1 = 45,  shape2 = 5),    # ~0.9 mean
  u_s   = rbeta(n_sims, shape1 = 30,  shape2 = 20),   # ~0.6 mean
  # Gamma for costs
  c_s   = rgamma(n_sims, shape = 100, rate = 1/300),  # ~30,000 mean
  c_drug= rgamma(n_sims, shape = 25,  rate = 1/400),  # ~10,000 mean
  dr    = 0.03
) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    # Simplified ICER calculation for each simulation
    dQALY = rnorm(1, mean = delta_qalys/n_start, sd = 50),
    dCost = rnorm(1, mean = delta_cost/n_start,  sd = 500),
    ICER  = dCost / dQALY
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Cost-effectiveness plane
wtp_threshold <- 100000   # ₹1,00,000 per QALY (illustrative)

ce_plane <- ggplot(psa_sims, aes(x = dQALY, y = dCost,
                                  colour = ICER < wtp_threshold)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  geom_abline(slope = wtp_threshold, intercept = 0,
              colour = "black", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "gray60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "gray60") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = col_well, "FALSE" = col_sick),
                      labels = c("TRUE" = "Cost-effective", "FALSE" = "Not cost-effective")) +
  annotate("text", x = max(psa_sims$dQALY)*0.7, y = max(psa_sims$dCost)*0.9,
           label = paste0("WTP = ₹", format(wtp_threshold, big.mark=","), "/QALY"),
           size = 3.5, colour = "gray30") +
  labs(title    = "Cost-Effectiveness Plane (PSA, n = 2,000 simulations)",
       subtitle = "Each dot = one simulation with sampled parameter values",
       x = "Incremental QALYs per person", y = "Incremental cost per person (₹)",
       colour = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0("₹", format(x, big.mark=","))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

# CEAC
wtp_range <- seq(0, 300000, by = 5000)
prob_ce   <- sapply(wtp_range, function(wtp) mean(psa_sims$ICER < wtp, na.rm=TRUE))

ceac <- ggplot(tibble(WTP = wtp_range, Prob = prob_ce), aes(x = WTP, y = Prob)) +
  geom_line(colour = col_well, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = wtp_threshold, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = col_sick, linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = wtp_threshold + 5000,
           y = prob_ce[which.min(abs(wtp_range - wtp_threshold))],
           label = sprintf("P(cost-effective) = %.0f%%",
                           prob_ce[which.min(abs(wtp_range - wtp_threshold))]*100),
           colour = col_sick, hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0("₹", format(x/1000, big.mark=","), "k")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  labs(title    = "Cost-Effectiveness Acceptability Curve (CEAC)",
       subtitle = "Probability the new treatment is cost-effective at each WTP threshold",
       x = "Willingness-to-pay threshold (₹/QALY)",
       y = "Probability cost-effective") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

gridExtra::grid.arrange(ce_plane, ceac, ncol = 2)

8 Part 8 — The “Five Layers” Summary

The Five Layers of a Cohort Markov Model
Layer What it answers In our model
  1. States
Where can the patient be? Well / Sick / Dead
  1. Transitions
Where can they go next? W<U+2192>W=88%, W<U+2192>S=10%, W<U+2192>D=2%, S<U+2192>S=80%, S<U+2192>D=20%
  1. Time
When does movement happen? 1-year cycle, 30-year horizon
  1. Values
What does each state cost and contribute in QALYs? Well: <U+20B9>5k, u=0.9; Sick: <U+20B9>30k, u=0.6; Dead: <U+20B9>0, u=0
  1. Decision
Which strategy is better? ICER = <U+0394>Cost / <U+0394>QALY

9 Part 9 — Critical Appraisal Checklist

When reading a published Markov model paper, ask these questions in order:

Critical Appraisal Checklist for Markov Model Papers
Step Question Red Flag if…
1 What are the health states? States are vague or clinically unmeaningful
2 Are states mutually exclusive and exhaustive? States overlap, or patients can fall ‘outside’ them
3 What transitions are allowed? Clinically important transitions are missing
4 Where do the transition probabilities come from? Single small trial; no uncertainty quantified
5 Is the cycle length appropriate for the disease? Cycle too long relative to important clinical events
6 What is the time horizon? Horizon ends before differences between strategies emerge
7 Does the model remember clinically important history? Time-dependent risk ignored; flat probability assumed
8 What cost is assigned to each state or event? Costs are undifferentiated or country-inappropriate
9 What utility is assigned to each state? Utilities not from the target patient population
10 Are future costs and outcomes discounted? No discounting; different rates for costs vs QALYs
11 How is uncertainty handled? Only one-way SA; no PSA; no structural alternatives tested
12 Was the model validated? No comparison with real-world survival or incidence
13 Were structural alternatives considered? Only parameters varied; structure never questioned
